generation.hypothesis: Incorporating microstructure-sensitive descriptors derived from the hierarchical heterostructure of HfNbTiVAl10 into a supervised machine-learning model will achieve at least a ~20% reduction in the prediction error for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related properties, as well as around a 30% decrease in computational time, compared to established continuum-based simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchically heterogeneous microstructure (multi-scale grains and phase distributions) in a homogenized condition.
generation.intervention: Training and applying a supervised machine-learning model on systematically acquired mechanical (tensile and fracture) and microstructural (phase fractions, grain size, and defect features) datasets for HfNbTiVAl10.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tension and fracture tests at varying strain rates, employing standardized sample geometries; microstructure characterized by imaging and compositional methods, with model training using partial datasets and validation on hold-out data.
generation.structural_mediator: Hierarchical phase arrangement and grain-size gradients in HfNbTiVAl10 serve as key model inputs that govern dislocation motion and crack initiation/propagation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Data-driven modeling captures non-linear dependencies between microstructure variations and mechanical response more effectively than classical continuum or simplified constitutive models, leveraging these hierarchical descriptors to predict performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional simulations, the machine-learning approach achieves roughly a 20% reduction in error in forecasting tensile modulus, yield stress, and fracture toughness, and demonstrates faster evaluation times by about 30%.
generation.baseline: Continuum-based or classical phenomenological models currently used to predict the mechanical properties of hierarchical high-entropy alloys under tension and fracture loading.
generation.boundary: Performance may degrade if the trained model is applied far outside the microstructural/process parameter range covered by the training data, such as significantly altered chemical composition or extreme thermomechanical treatments.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative estimates of improvement (20%-level accuracy gains, 30%-level speed gains) are tentative and rely on dataset fidelity and completeness; unpredictable compositional or microstructural transitions could reduce ML effectiveness.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model predictions deviate from these new, independently measured mechanical properties by significantly more than the targeted ~20% reduction in error, then the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: We employ machine learning (ML) to predict the yield stress and plastic strain of body-centered cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the compression test. Our machine learning model leverages currently available databases of BCC and BCC+B2 entropy alloys, using feature engineering to capture electronic factors, atomic ordering from mixing enthalpy, and the D parameter related to stacking fault energy. The model achieves low Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE). Utilizing Random Forest Regression (RFR) and Genetic Algorithms for feature selection, our model excels in both predictive accuracy and interpretability. Rigorous 10-fold cross-validation ensures robust generalization. Our discussion delves into feature importance, highlighting key predictors and their impact on mechanical properties. This work provides an important step toward designing high-performance structural high-entropy alloys, providing a powerful tool for predicting mechanical properties and identifying new alloys with superior strength and ductility.

AbstractThis study introduces a language transformer-based machine learning model to predict key mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), addressing the challenges due to their complex, multi-principal element compositions and limited experimental data. By pre-training the transformer on extensive synthetic materials data and fine-tuning it with specific HEA datasets, the model effectively captures intricate elemental interactions through self-attention mechanisms. This approach mitigates data scarcity issues via transfer learning, enhancing predictive accuracy for properties like elongation (%) and ultimate tensile strength compared to traditional regression models such as random forests and Gaussian processes. The model’s interpretability is enhanced by visualizing attention weights, revealing significant elemental relationships that align with known metallurgical principles. This work demonstrates the potential of transformer models to accelerate materials discovery and optimization, enabling accurate property predictions, thereby advancing the field of materials informatics. In this study, three popular ML methods, namely random forest regressor, gradient boosting regressor, and decision tree regression models, were used for predicting the elastic properties of RCCAs. The ML model consists of eight different descriptors of RCCAs. GBR performs very well as compared with the other two ML models. While predicting elastic constants C11, C12, and C44, the R2 value of testing data of the GBR model were 0.97, 0.803, and 0.787, respectively. The GBR model has a high R2 value and low MAE and RMSE error than RF and XGB ML models and is promising for predicting the elastic constant of RHEAs. The elastic constants of alloys MoNbTiVZr, MoNbTiZr, NbTiVZr, and NbTaTiV predicted by the GBR model are consistent with the current simulation and experimental findings, which validate its prediction accuracy and applicability. The feature importance from SHAP and PCP plot shows that the VEC and MT are the most influential features affecting the elastic constants of RHEAs. The dataset created in this study using CALPHAD and DFT modeling could help scientists to construct RHEAs that can endure extreme temperatures and pressures.
